text: Conservation of Energy The terms conserved quantity and conservation law have specific scientific meanings in physics. In everyday usage you could conserve water by not using it, using less of it, or reusing it. In scientific usage a conserved quantity for a system stays constant, changes by a definite amount that is transferred to other systems and or is converted into other forms of that quantity. There are no other forms of water where it's all H2O. Nor is there any physical law of conservation that is specific to water. Systems with a single particle Consider a system with a single particle where system is used pretty loosely here. In section 8.1 we showed that the work done on a particle can be represented as the negative change in the potential energy, equation 8.1, or the change in kinetic energy, equation 8.3. For a conservative system the sum of the changes in kinetic and potential energy were equal to zero. That is change in K plus change in U equals zero in section 8.1.3.3. We expand this idea to include non-conservative forces and to define the mechanical energy of the particle. Conservation of energy The mechanical energy E of a particle stays constant unless external or non-conservative forces do work on it. The change in mechanical energy is equal to the work done from A to B. By the non-conservative forces W sub NC comma AB or W sub NC comma AB equals change in K plus U comma AB equals change in E comma AB. This expression describes the concept of energy conservation for a classical particle, which is a point mass moves at non-relativistic speed and obeys Newton's laws of motion. We can recover the prior expression when there are no non-conservative forces or the non-conservative forces do no work. In this case we have W sub NC comma AB equals change in E comma AB equals zero. Zero equals change in K plus U comma AB equals K sub B minus K sub A plus U sub B minus U sub A. K sub A plus U sub A equals K sub B plus U sub B. Checkmark problem solving strategy, conservation of energy. First, identify bodies within the system. Second, identify all forces acting on each body. Third, determine whether there are conservative or non-conservative forces doing work. Set W sub NC comma AB equals zero if they are all conservative sources of work. Otherwise, W sub NC comma AB equals change in E comma AB. Fourth, for every conservative force that does work, choose a reference point and determine the respective potential function of each. Fifth, if only conservative work is done, set the sum of kinetic and potential energies at point A equal to the sum of those energies at point B. You can use conservation of energy to calculate the speed of a particle at particular points in its motion. More advanced treatments allow you to calculate the full time dependence of a particle's motion for a given potential energy. Consider a particle moving in one dimension with a potential energy U of X with only conservative interactions, i.e. no friction. Then we can use the total energy to describe the kinetic energy K and the speed V in a different way. Mathematically, this is given by E equals K plus U of X. K equals 1 over 2 MV squared equals E minus U of X. V equals square root of 2 over M times E minus U of X. Recalling the definition of velocity as V equals DX over DT, we can separate the variables and integrate. DT equals DX over V. T equals integral 0 to the power of T DT equals integral X0 to the power of X DX over square root of 2 times E minus U of X over M. If you can do the final integral with respect to DX, then you can solve for X as a function of T. Example problem, simple pendulum. The problem. A particle of mass M is hung from the ceiling by a massless string of length 1.0 meters as shown in figure. The particle is released from rest when the angle between the string and the downward vertical direction is 30 degrees. What is its speed when it reaches the lowest point of its arc? The worked solution follows. The model. The system consists of the particle and the earth so that gravitational potential energy is internal to the system. The string is massless and constrains the particle to move on a circular arc of radius L equals 1.0 meters. Air resistance is neglected. The string tension does no work on the particle because the tension force is always directed along the string while the displacement is tangent to the arc. So the tension is perpendicular to the instantaneous displacement. The only force that does work is gravity, which is conservative, so mechanical energy is conserved. The gravitational potential energy is defined to be 0 at the lowest point of the swing. The particle is released from rest at an initial angle theta equals 30 degrees measured from the downward vertical. So the initial mechanical energy is purely gravitational potential energy determined by the vertical height above the lowest point. The math. Because only conservative work is done on the particle earth system, mechanical energy is conserved. So the total mechanical energy at release equals the total mechanical energy at the lowest point. The particle starts from rest, so its initial kinetic energy is 0, and at the lowest point, the gravitational potential energy is defined to be 0. Conservation of energy therefore requires that the initial gravitational potential energy equals the final kinetic energy, which gives MGH equals 1 over 2 MV squared. The height H is found from the geometry of a circle of radius L. At the release angle theta O, the vertical distance from the pivot to the particle is L cosine theta O, while at the lowest point that vertical distance is L. So the particle is higher than the lowest point by H equals L minus L cosine theta O equals L times 1 minus cosine theta O. Substituting this height into the energy equation and canceling M gives GH equals 1 over 2 times V squared. MGL times 1 minus cosine theta O equals 1 half MV squared. V equals the square root of 2GL times 1 minus cosine theta O. Substituting G equals 9.81 meters per second squared. L equals 1.0 meters, and theta O equals 30 degrees. Yields V equals the square root of 2 times 9.81 meters per second squared times 1.0 meters times 1 minus cosine 30 degrees. Yields V equals 1.62 meters per second. The conclusion. The particle's speed at the lowest point of its arc is 1.62 meters per second. This result follows from conservation of mechanical energy using the vertical height change implied by the pendulum geometry, and defining gravitational potential energy to be 0 at the lowest point. Example problem. Air resistance on a falling object. The problem. A helicopter is hovering at an altitude of 1 kilometer when a panel from its underside breaks loose and plummets to the ground, figure. The mass of the panel is 15 kilograms, and it hits the ground with a speed of 45 meters per second. How much mechanical energy was dissipated by air resistance during the panel's descent? The worked solution. The model. The system consists of the panel and the earth. Gravity is a conservative force, while air resistance is a non-conservative force that makes negative work during the fall. The panel is released from rest at an altitude of 1 kilometer and reaches the ground with a known speed, so the dissipated mechanical energy can be found from the change in the system's mechanical energy. The gravitational potential energy is defined to be 0 at ground level. The energy dissipated by air resistance is taken to be the magnitude of the non-conservative work, which equals the decrease in mechanical energy from the initial state to the final state. The math. The change in mechanical energy between the initial state i and the final state f is related to the non-conservative work by W sub nc i f equals change in k plus u sub i f. k sub f plus u sub f minus k sub i plus u sub i. Because air resistance dissipates energy, the dissipated mechanical energy is the magnitude of this work, so change in e sub dis equals the magnitude of W sub nc i f. At release, the panel starts from rest, so k sub i equals 0. The gravitational potential energy is defined to be 0 at the ground, so u sub f equals 0, and u sub i equals mgh with h equals 1,000 meters. The final kinetic energy is k sub f equals 1 half mv squared with v equals 45 meters per second. Substituting these expressions gives W sub nc i f equals 1 half mv squared minus 0 minus 0 plus mgh equals 1 half mv squared minus mgh. Using m equals 15 kilograms, v equals 45 meters per second, g equals 9.81 meters per second squared, and h equals 1,000 meters yields W sub nc i f equals 1 half 15 kilograms times 45 meters per second squared, minus 15 kilograms times 9.81 meters per second squared. So, the second second squared times 1,000 meters equals minus 1.32 times 10 to the fifth joules. Therefore, the mechanical energy dissipated by air resistance is change in e sub dis equals W sub nc i f equals 1.32 times 10 to the fifth joules equals 132 kilojoules. Air resistance dissipated 132 kilojoules of mechanical energy during the panel's fall. This equals the decrease in the system's mechanical energy from the initial state at 1 kilometer altitude to the final state at the ground. Example problem, constant acceleration, the problem. Use the potential energy u of x equals e x divided by x sub o for e greater than 0 in equation to find the position x of a particle as a function of time t. The worked solution follows the model. The system consists of a particle undergoing one-dimensional motion along the x-axis under the influence of a conservative force derived from the given potential energy function. The potential energy varies linearly with position, so the corresponding force is constant. The particle starts from rest at position x sub o and moves under this constant force without the influence of any non-conservative forces. Mechanical energy is conserved allowing the motion to be analyzed using the energy time relation given in equation. The math. The energy time relation for one-dimensional motion under a conservative force can be written as t equals integral sub x sub o to the x sub i dx over square root of 2 over m times e minus u of x. Substituting u of x equals e times x over x sub o into this expression gives t equals integral sub x sub o to the power of x dx over square root of 2 e over m times 1 minus x over x sub o. Equals 1 over square root of 2 e over m x sub o integral sub x sub o to the power of x dx over square root of x sub o minus x equals negative 2 square root of x sub o minus x over square root of 2 e over m x sub o. Solving this expression for the position as a function of time yields x of t equals x sub o minus 1 over 2 times e over m x sub o t squared. The conclusion. The particle's position varies quadratically with time according to x of t equals x sub o minus 1 over 2 times e over m x sub o t squared. This corresponds to motion starting from rest at x sub o with a constant acceleration directed toward decreasing x. Systems with several particles. Systems generally consist of multiple particles. To apply conservation of energy to such a system, you just have to include the kinetic energy, k sub i, and potential energy, u sub i of all the particles, and the work done by the non-conservative forces acting on them. In this case, we have the sum of w sub non-conservative a b equals the sum from i equals 1 to n of delta times the quantity k sub i plus u sub i from a to b.
